content: Gingivitis, also known as inflammation of the gums, is a condition caused by bacterial biofilms, commonly referred to as dental plaque, that adhere to the surfaces of teeth. This condition is characterized by localized, reversible inflammation of the gingiva without any detectable loss of bone or clinical attachment. It is a common condition that affects individuals of all ages, from children to adults, and is frequently observed during dental examinations. The etiology of gingivitis is multifactorial, involving a combination of factors such as poor oral hygiene, genetic predisposition, socioeconomic status, demographic influences, iatrogenic factors, and behavioral habits. These factors often act synergistically, complicating the identification of specific risk factors. Gingivitis is initiated by substances derived from microbial plaque that accumulate at or near the gingival sulcus. Other local and systemic factors may either enhance plaque accumulation or retention or increase the susceptibility of gingival tissues to microbial attack. This leads to an inflammatory response that initially presents as edema and may progress to fibrosis if the condition persists. The earliest clinical sign of gingival inflammation is the transudation of gingival fluid, which is initially a thin cellular transudate but is later replaced by a fluid containing serum and leukocytes. The redness of the gingival margin is partly due to the aggregation and enlargement of blood vessels in the subepithelial connective tissue and the loss of keratinization on the facial aspects of the gingiva. Despite these changes, gingivitis is often painless and rarely causes spontaneous bleeding, making it difficult for patients to recognize the condition. However, gingivitis is clinically significant as it is considered a precursor to periodontitis, a more severe condition characterized by gingival inflammation, connective tissue attachment loss, and bone loss. Gingivitis is a reversible condition, and treatment primarily focuses on controlling the causative or risk factors to reduce or eliminate inflammation and repair the gingival tissues. Proper periodontal maintenance through personal and professional care is essential to prevent recurrences. Simple gingivitis can be managed with adequate oral hygiene measures, such as regular brushing and flossing, with or without the use of antibacterial mouth rinses, and thorough scaling performed by a dental professional using hand or ultrasonic instruments. Classification of Gingivitis The classification of gingival diseases has undergone several updates over the years. In 2017, the American Academy of Periodontology and the European Federation of Periodontology co-sponsored the World Workshop on the Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases and Conditions. This workshop updated the previous classification established in 1999. Gingivitis is diagnosed based on the presence of gingival inflammation at one or more sites and bleeding on probing as the primary diagnostic parameter. Stages of Gingivitis Gingivitis progresses through four distinct stages, as first described by Page and Schroeder in 1976, before potentially advancing to periodontitis if left untreated. Pathophysiology Gingivitis typically originates from bacterial plaque that accumulates in the spaces between the gums and teeth, as well as visible calculus (tartar) formed on the teeth. When teeth are not adequately cleaned through regular brushing and flossing, bacterial plaque accumulates and becomes mineralized by calcium and other minerals in saliva, forming a hard material called calculus. This calculus harbors bacteria and irritates the gingiva. As the bacterial plaque biofilm thickens, an anaerobic environment develops, allowing more pathogenic bacteria to thrive, release toxins, and initiate gingival inflammation. Excessive injury to the gums, such as from overly vigorous brushing, can also contribute to a cycle of recession, inflammation, and infection. In some cases, the immune system may become weakened due to local or systemic conditions, exacerbating the infection. Over time, this inflammation and infection can lead to the formation of deep pockets between the teeth and gums, as well as bone loss, ultimately resulting in periodontitis. Local Factors Crowded teeth make it difficult to remove plaque completely. Malaligned teeth often require orthodontic correction, which can further complicate cleaning. Poorly fitted or improperly finished dental prostheses can act as a nidus for plaque accumulation. In children, eruptive gingivitis is associated with tooth eruption, as plaque tends to accumulate in areas where primary teeth are exfoliating or permanent teeth are erupting, making oral hygiene maintenance challenging. Infectious Gingivitis Low-grade injuries to local tissues, such as fractured teeth, overhanging restorations, overextended denture flanges, and faulty fixed dental prostheses, can predispose individuals to gingivitis. Hypersensitive Reaction Allergens in products such as chewing gum, toothpaste, cinnamon, mint, or red pepper can trigger plasma cell infiltration in the gingiva, leading to plasma cell gingivitis. Nutritional Gingivitis Dietary habits involving high intake of refined carbohydrates and an increased omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acid ratio can activate inflammatory processes through NF-kB activation and oxidative stress. Hormonal Gingivitis This form of gingivitis occurs during pregnancy, puberty, or steroid therapy, even in the absence of plaque. For example: Pregnancy: Elevated levels of circulating female sex hormones can lead to pregnancy gingivitis. Puberty: Gingivitis is observed earlier in girls (ages 11–13) compared to boys (ages 13–14) due to the presence of estrogen and testosterone receptors in gingival cells. Drug-Induced Gingivitis Certain drugs can induce gingival inflammation by promoting fibroblast proliferation or causing an imbalance in the synthesis and degradation of the extracellular matrix, leading to the accumulation of immature proteins, particularly collagen. Causes The etiology of gingivitis is multifactorial, involving local, systemic, genetic, and behavioral factors that often act synergistically. The most common cause is inadequate oral hygiene, which leads to dental plaque formation. Epidemiology and Demographics Gingivitis is the most common periodontal disease worldwide, affecting individuals of all age groups. It occurs in approximately half of the population by the age of 4 or 5 years, with prevalence peaking at nearly 100% during puberty. However, the incidence declines slightly after puberty and remains constant into adulthood. Gingivitis is more prevalent in males, likely due to better oral care practices among females. Pregnant women are more prone to severe forms of gingivitis compared to non-pregnant women. Additionally, individuals of lower socioeconomic status are more commonly affected due to limited access to healthcare and less emphasis on oral hygiene. Risk Factors Common risk factors for gingivitis include poor oral hygiene, smoking, stress, nutritional deficiencies, systemic conditions (e.g., diabetes, HIV/AIDS), and certain medications. Complications If left untreated, gingivitis can lead to: Recurrence of gingivitis Periodontitis Infection or abscess of the gingiva or jawbones Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG), also known as trench mouth Clinical Presentation Gingivitis can present as acute or chronic inflammation, which may be localized or generalized. It is categorized into: Marginal gingivitis: Inflammation confined to the gingival margin. Papillary gingivitis: Inflammation of the interdental papillae. Diffuse gingivitis: Extensive involvement of the gingival margin, attached gingiva, and interdental papillae. Symptoms Symptoms of gingivitis include swollen gums, mouth sores, bright red or purple gums, shiny gums, painless gums (except when pressure is applied), bleeding gums during brushing or flossing, itching gums, and receding gum lines. Diagnosis Diagnosis involves a detailed history review and physical examination. Clinical evaluation includes assessing erythematous and friable tissue at the gum margins. Pocket depths around each tooth should be measured, with depths greater than 3 mm indicating a higher risk of gingivitis or periodontitis. Laboratory tests and radiographs are not routinely required but may be used to rule out other conditions. Treatment Treatment aims to restore inflamed tissues to clinical health and prevent progression to periodontitis. A dentist or dental hygienist will perform thorough cleaning, including scaling to remove biofilm and deposits, and may use laser decontamination if available. Oral hygiene reinforcement, such as twice-daily brushing, daily interdental cleaning, and the use of adjunctive chemical plaque control agents, is essential. Modifiable systemic or local factors should be addressed, such as changing medications, prescribing supplements for nutritional deficiencies, or replacing faulty prostheses. In severe cases, oral antibiotics may be prescribed. Prevention Maintaining good oral hygiene is key to preventing gingivitis. Patients should be educated on proper brushing techniques, the importance of flossing, and the use of antiseptic mouthwashes. Regular dental visits for professional cleaning and monitoring are recommended, especially for individuals with systemic conditions predisposing them to gingivitis. A balanced diet and awareness of risk factors such as age, smoking, and genetics are also important preventive measures.
